### a. Definitions {.unnumbered}

#### Classic causal inference



::: {#def-random-variable .theorem}
# Random variable

A random *scalar* quantity assumed to be behave according some unkown probability distribution.

:::


::: {#def-statistical-model .theorem}
## Statistical model

A collection of probability distributions on a vector of random variables $\mathbf V$. Probability distributions in this model are characterized using a set of parameters $\mathbf \theta$.

$$
\mathcal{M}=\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\quad\text{on set of random variables }\mathbf V.
$$
:::

::: {#def-npsem .theorem}
## Non-parametric structural equation model \[NPSEM\]

A [statistical model](#def-statistical-model) characterized by a set of deterministic functions called structural equations. Each structural equation $f_V$ returns the value of a random variable $V$ in the model. It is a function of the other random variables as well as a random error term $U$: 

$$
\theta =\{f_{V}(\mathbf V_{-V}, U_V):V\in\mathbf V\}.
$$

By definition, no random variable is directly or indirectly a function of itself. We can order the random variables and write each as a function of prior random variables: 

$$
V_{j} \;=\; f_{V_j}\!\big( V_{1},\dots,V_{j-1},\, U_{V_j} \big).
$$

:::

::: {#def-npsem-ie .theorem}
## NPSEM with independent errors \[NPSEM-IE\]

An [NPSEM](#def-npsem) with mutually independent error terms.


$$
j\neq k  \iff  U_j \perp U_k 
$$
:::

::: {#def-parent .theorem}
## Parent

A random variable $X$ is a parent to random variable $Y$ if $X$ appears in the [structural equation](#def-npsem) for $Y$. The set of parents for $X$ is denoted $\mathbf{Pa}(X)$.

:::


::: {#def-observational-unit .theorem}
## Observational unit

A sub-vector of $\mathscr{O}_i, i \in [1,n]$ of the random variables $\mathbf V$ such that:

$$
\mathbf V = \big[ \mathscr{O}_1, ..., \mathscr{O}_n\big]^T
$$

:::


::: {#def-equivalence .theorem}
## Equivalence

Two random variables are equivalent across observations if they belong to different [observational units](#def-observational-unit) but represent the same construct. 

$$
X_i\sim X_j\iff \ X_i\in  \mathscr{O}_i;\ X_j\in  \mathscr{O}_j,\ X_i \text{ same construct } X_j \ (i\ne j).
$$
 
 


:::










::: {#def-no-spillover .theorem}
## No spillover assumption

The assumption that no variable is a [parent](#def-parent-child) of an [equivalent](#def-equivalence) variable in another [observational unit](#def-observational-unit).


$$
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(X')\quad
\forall\, X\sim X',\ X\in \mathscr O_i,\ X'\in \mathscr O_j,\ i\ne j.
$$
:::

::: {#def-no-interference .theorem}
## No interference assumption 

The assumption that no variable is a [parent](#def-parent-child) of a [non-equivalent](#def-equivalence) variable in another [observational unit](#def-observational-unit).


$$
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(Y)\quad
\forall\, X\in \mathscr O_i,\ Y\in \mathscr O_j,\ X\not\sim Y \ i\ne j
$$
:::

::: {#def-identical-distributions .theorem}
## Identical distributions assumption


The assumption that [equivalent](#def-equivalence) variables have identical [structural equations](#def-npsem).


$$
X_i\sim X_j\Rightarrow f_{X_i}=f_{X_j}.
$$
:::



::: {#def-intervention .theorem}
## Intervention equation

An intervention equation in relation to random variable $V$ is a deterministic function $h$ with the same inputs and outputs as the structural equation for $V$. 
:::

::: {#def-intervention-regime .theorem}
## Intervention regime


A set of  intervention equations defined on a subset of random variables $\mathbf E \subset \mathbf V$.

$$
\Gamma = \{ h_V \}_{V \in \mathbf{E}} 
$$


:::




::: {#def-interventional-npsem .theorem}
# Interventional NPSEM

An NPSEM $\mathcal{M}$ for which a subset of structural equations $\mathbf E$ have been replaced by intervention equations in intervention regime $\Gamma$. 


$$
\mathcal{M}^{(\Gamma)} =  \{f_V^{(\Gamma)}: V \in \mathbf V \}
$$


$$
f_V^{(\Gamma)} = \begin{cases}
  h_V & \text{if}  & V \in \mathbf E\\
  f_V & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$


:::



::: {#def-causal-model .theorem}
## Causal model

A causal model $\mathcal C$ of NPSEM $\mathcal M$ under intervention $\Gamma$ is an NPSEM that is generated by combining $\mathcal M$ with its interventional NPSEMs $\mathcal M^{(\Gamma_1)}...\mathcal M^{(\Gamma_q)}$ and setting the error terms equal for variables that assume the same role across these models. Assuming $\mathcal M$ is a model of random vector $\mathbf V$:

$$
\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{M} \cup \mathcal M^{(\Gamma_1)} \cup ... \cup \mathcal M^{(\Gamma_q)}
$$


$$
\text{for all } V \in \mathbf V, \quad {U_V} = {U}^{(\Gamma_1)}_V = ... = {U}^{(\Gamma_q)}_V
$$




:::

::: {#def-ffrcistg .theorem}
## FFRCISTG model

A finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (FFRCISTG) is a causal model of an NPSEM-IE $\mathcal M$ under intervention regime $\Gamma$. By assumption, $\mathcal M$ satisfies: (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [no interference](#def-no-interference), and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions). 


:::

#### Network causal inference


::: {#def-graph .theorem}
## Graph

An ordered pair $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$ with nodeset $\mathcal{N}$and adjacency function $\psi$. The adjacecy function assigns a nonnegative weight to each unordered pair of nodes $(i,j)$. 

$$
\mathscr G=(\mathcal N,\psi),\qquad
\psi:\mathcal N\times\mathcal N\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0},\qquad
\psi(i,j)=\psi(j,i)
$$

Nodes $i,j \in \mathcal{N}$ are connected if and only if $\psi(i,j) > 0$.
:::


::: {#def-neighborhood .theorem}
## Neighborhood

The set of nodes connected to a given node $i \in \mathcal{N}$ in [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$.

$$
\mathcal{N}_i = \{ j \in \mathcal{N} : \psi(i,j) > 0 \}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-network-weights-vector .theorem}
## Network weights 


The vector representing the edges a given node $i$ shares with other nodes in [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$.

$$
\Psi_i = [\psi(i,1), \dots, \psi(i,n)]^T
\qquad n=|\mathcal N|.
$$
:::

::: {#def-network-values .theorem}
## Network values 

The sub-vector of some $\mathbf X \in \{0,1\}^n$ that is related to nodes in the [neighborhood](#def-neighborhood) of $i$ in [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)$ 


$$
\mathbf X_{\mathcal N_i}=\big(X_j\big)_{j\in \mathcal N_i}
$$
:::

::: {#def-exposure-mapping .theorem}
## Exposure mapping

A function $g_i : \{0,1\}^{K \times n} \to \mathbb{R}^m$

such that

$$
Y_i = f_{Y_i}\big(g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K), U_{Y_i}\big).
$$

where $f_{Y_i}$ is the [structural equation](#def-npsem) for $Y_i$, and $\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K \in \{0,1\}^n$ are the [parents](#def-parent-child) of $Y_i$ in some [NPSEM](#def-npsem) $\mathcal{M}$ 
:::

::: {#def-separability .theorem}
## Separability

The assumption that an [exposure mapping](#def-exposure-mapping) $g_i$ can be written:

$$
g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K) 
  = \big[ \begin{pmatrix} X_{1i} \\ \dots \\ X_{Ki} \end{pmatrix},\, g_{1i}(\mathbf{X}_1),\, \dots,\, g_{Ki}(\mathbf{X}_K)\big]^T,
$$

where each $g_{ti} : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a *component function* of $g_i$. A structural equation is said to be separable if its exposure mapping is separable. 
:::



::: {#def-positional-invariance .theorem}
## Positional invariance
The assumption that a [component function](#def-separability) $g_{ti}$ obtains the same value up to a re-ordering of its the network value for its inputs related network weights vector. i.e. $g_{ti}$ is [positionally invariant](#def-positional-invariance) with respect to $\mathscr{G}_t$ if for all $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X}' \in \{0,1\}^n$


$$
\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}'_{\mathcal{N}_j}, 
\quad 
\Psi_{i,\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\Psi_{j,\mathcal{N}_j}
\Rightarrow
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) = g_{tj}(\mathbf{X}').
$$

An exposure mapping shows positional invariance with respect to  $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ if it is separable and all its component functions show positional invariance with respect to an element of  $\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$. A structural equation is positionally invariant if its exposure mapping is positionally invariant. 
:::

::: {#def-boundedness .theorem}
## Boundedness

The assumption that a component function $g_{ti}$ can only take on values from a finite set. i.e. $g_{ti}$ is bounded if there exists a finite set $\mathcal{D}$ and a constant $c$ such that for $\mathbf{X} \in \{0,1\}^n$

$$
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) \in \mathcal{D} \quad \text{ for }|\mathcal{D}|< c \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

An exposure mapping is bounded if it is [separable](#def-separability) and all its component functions are bounded. 
:::

::: {#def-network-exposure-mapping .theorem}
## Network exposure mapping

A [component function](#def-separability) $g_{ti}$  which is [bounded](#def-boundedness) and [positionally invariant](#def-positional-invariance) with respect to some [graph](#def-graph) $\mathscr{G}_t$. 

:::

::: {#def-homogeneous-network-interference .theorem}
## Homogeneous network interference

The assumption that an exposure mapping $g_{ti}$ is separable and all its [component functions](#def-separability) are [network exposure mappings](#def-network-exposure-mapping). An NPSEM satisfies homogenous network interference if all its exposure mappings satisfy homogenous network interference. 


:::



::: {#def-network-ffrcistg .theorem}
##  NFFRCISTG model

A network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (NFFRCISTG) is a causal model of an NPSEM-IE $\mathcal M$ under intervention regime $\Gamma$. By assumption, $\mathcal M$ satisfies: (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [homogenous network interference](#def-no-interference), and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions). 


:::

#### Social and spatial inference


::: {#def-graph-generator .theorem}
# Random graph generator

An $n \times n$ function whose entries $\psi(i,j)$ are each a deterministic symmetric function of the other variables in the model along with an error term. 

$$
\psi(i,j) = f_{\psi_{ij}}(\mathbf{Pa}(\psi(i,j)), U_{\psi_{ij}})
$$

such that 

$$
U_{\psi_{ij}} = U_{\psi_{ji}} \text{ and } f_{\psi_{ij}} = f_{\psi_{ji}}
$$


:::

::: {#def-random-graph-npsem .theorem}
## NPSEM-NI

An NPSEM with networked errors is an NPSEM which includes random graph generators among the structural equations. Error terms are correlated within each graph generator but independent across graph generators, between structural equations and graph generators, and between structural equations. 


:::

::: {#def-homogenous-random-network-interference .theorem}
# Homogenous random network interference

An exposure mapping exhibits homogeneous random network interference with respect to a [random graph set](#def-random-graph) $\{\psi_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ if it is separable and all its [component functions](#def-separability) are [network exposure mappings](#def-network-exposure-mapping). An NPSEM exhibiits homogenous random network interference if all its exposure mappings exhibit homogenous randomn network interference. 

:::


::: {#def-social-spatial-ffrcistg .theorem}
## RNFFRCISTG

A random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (RNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a [random graph NPSEM-IE](#def-random-graph-npsem ) which satisfies the (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [homogenous random network interference](#def-homogenous-random-network-interference), and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions) assumptions.
:::


::: {#def-random-graph-npsem .theorem}
## Random bipartite graph NPSEM

A random bipartite graph NPSEM is a random graph NPSEM which whose generators produce bipartite graphs. 

 

:::








::: {#def-social-spatial-ffrcistg .theorem}
## BRNFFRCISTG model

A bipartite random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (BRNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a [bipartite random graph NPSEM-IE](#def-bipartite-random-graph-npsem ) which satisfies the (1) [no spillover](#def-no-spillover), (2) [homogenous random network interference](#def-homogenous-random-network-interference), and (3) [identical distributions](#def-identical-distributions) assumptions.


:::
